title: Chapter 111 — The Store's Money: Margins, Costs & The P&L
intro: How the store actually makes money and reading its health.

sections.title: The P&L Structure
sections.content:
Revenue minus Cost of Goods Sold equals Gross Profit. Gross Profit minus Operating Expenses equals Operating Profit. Operating Profit minus interest, taxes, and depreciation equals Net Profit.

The numbers that matter for a floor manager: Gross Margin percentage — are we pricing correctly? Are we discounting too much? Labour as percentage of revenue — are we overstaffed or understaffed? Revenue per employee — productivity metric.

sections.title: Margin vs Markup
sections.content:
These are NOT the same thing. Confusing them costs stores thousands.

Markup is the percentage added on top of cost: cost $1,000, sell $1,400, markup is 40 percent. Margin is the percentage of selling price that is profit: same sale, margin is 28.6 percent.

If your manager says 'maintain 30 percent margin' and you apply a 30 percent markup, you are at 23 percent margin. You just lost 7 points of profit on every sale.

The conversion: 25 percent markup equals 20 percent margin. 33 percent markup equals 25 percent margin. 50 percent markup equals 33 percent margin. 100 percent markup equals 50 percent margin.

sections.title: Why Attach Margin Matters
sections.content:
Appliance margins are thin: 18-32 percent. Attach margins are rich: warranties at 50-70 percent, installation at 40-60 percent, accessories at 45-65 percent.

A $100K month at 28 percent margin with $22K in expenses equals $6K profit. A $100K month at 32 percent margin with $22K in expenses equals $10K profit. That 4 percentage points of margin improvement nearly doubled the profit. And the easiest way to increase overall margin is to increase the attach rate — because attach products have 2-3 times the margin of appliances.
